competitions.name: NanoGPT Speedrun (modded-nanogpt)
competitions.tagline: Train a GPT-2-class LM to a target FineWeb val loss as fast as possible on 8xH100.
competitions.description: A competitive speedrun where contributors submit training-algorithm changes that reach a fixed cross-entropy loss target on the FineWeb validation set in the least wallclock time (Track 1, GPT-2 Small at 3.28 loss) or the fewest optimizer steps (Track 3). Track 2 targets GPT-2 Medium at 2.92 loss. Records are validated by re-running on 8xH100 hardware (sponsored by PrimeIntellect) and merged via PR; the repo maintains a full historical leaderboard of world records.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to master adding a record folder under records/track_1_short/ (or track_2_medium/, track_3_optimization/) with the modified train_gpt.py and run logs demonstrating the new record.
participation.submissionFormat: Modified train_gpt.py plus run logs (main.log / *.txt) showing val loss and timing; statistical significance p<0.01 that mean val loss ≤ target.
participation.computeDetails: Official records are timed on 8x NVIDIA H100 GPUs from PrimeIntellect. Track 3 allows unlimited wallclock budget (step count is the metric).
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; contributors credited in README and record history.
participation.verification: Peer validation via PR review; records must be reproducible on the same hardware and beat the prior record when baselined.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt.git && cd modded-nanogpt
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install torch==2.10 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python data/cached_fineweb10B.py 9
./run.sh

competitions.name: StarVLA
competitions.tagline: A Lego-like open-source codebase for developing, training, and evaluating Vision-Language-Action models on robot benchmarks.
competitions.description: StarVLA is a modular research platform for building Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, with pluggable VLM backbones, interchangeable action heads (FAST, OFT, PI, GR00T), and benchmark-agnostic deployment hooks. It integrates a broad set of simulation and real-robot benchmarks (LIBERO, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin, DOMINO, BEHAVIOR, CALVIN, RoboDojo, VLA-Arena, MetaWorld, Evo-DexBench) and reports SOTA results. The project is maintained by the StarVLA Community and released under the MIT License.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to the repository following the contributing guidelines in docs/CONTRIBUTING.md; run Black + Ruff on changed files before submitting.
participation.submissionFormat: Code contributions (new framework variants, benchmark integrations, bug fixes) as pull requests; benchmark results documented in READMEs and model_zoo.md.
participation.computeDetails: Training typically uses multi-GPU setups (e.g., 8 processes with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2/3); can run on a single A100 with smaller VLMs like Florence-2.
participation.eligibility: Open to the community; MIT License permits commercial use, modification, and distribution.
participation.verification: Human review of pull requests; benchmark results reported by contributors.

competitions.name: AssetOpsBench
competitions.tagline: Build and evaluate industrial AI agents that turn operational evidence into reliable maintenance actions.
competitions.description: AssetOpsBench is an open ecosystem and benchmark for industrial AI agents, with 141 expert-curated scenarios spanning sensing, reasoning, and action across asset operations. Agents connect to domain MCP servers (IoT, failure modes, time-series, work orders, vibration) and are scored against expert-defined ground-truth trajectories using LLM-as-judge and static JSON scorers. It is run by IBM Research and has hosted public competitions (CODS 2025, IJCAI 2026) with leaderboards on Codabench and Kaggle.

participation.howToSubmit: Run an agent against the scenario suite and submit results; for scenario contributions, open a PR or issue tagged `new-scenario` following the utterance and ground-truth guidelines.
participation.submissionFormat: Agent trajectories (JSON) plus evaluation reports; new scenarios as PRs with utterance and ground-truth files.
participation.computeDetails: MCP servers and CouchDB run locally via Docker; LLM inference is via API (LiteLLM proxy / TokenRouter).
participation.eligibility: Open to researchers, engineers, educators, students, and domain experts.
participation.verification: Offline evaluation with LLM-as-judge and static_json scorers; competition tracks use public and hidden evaluation.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/IBM/AssetOpsBench.git
cd AssetOpsBench
pip install -e .
uv sync
cp .env.public .env
uv run evaluate --trajectories traces/trajectories --scenarios /path/to/scenarios_data --scorer-default static_json --reports-dir reports/static_json_eval

problems.description: Agents complete 141 expert-curated industrial operations scenarios (99 single-agent, 42 multi-agent) by coordinating MCP tools over IoT, failure-mode, time-series, work-order, and vibration data. Scored against expert ground-truth trajectories via LLM-as-judge and static JSON scorers.
problems.name: Industrial Asset Operations Agent Scenarios

competitions.name: AlpacaEval
competitions.tagline: Maximize LLM win rate against a reference model, judged by an automatic GPT-4 annotator.
competitions.description: AlpacaEval is an automatic evaluator for instruction-following LLMs. Models are scored by the fraction of times a strong LLM annotator (e.g. GPT-4) prefers their outputs over a reference model's outputs on the 805-example AlpacaEval set. AlpacaEval 2.0 uses gpt4_turbo as baseline and a length-controlled win rate to debias for output length. Maintained by the tatsu-lab group (Stanford); contributions are merged via pull requests to the GitHub repo and reflected on the public leaderboard website.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, add a model config under src/alpaca_eval/models_configs/<model_name>, run `alpaca_eval evaluate_from_model --model_configs '<model_name>'`, then open a PR adding the config, results/<model_name>/model_outputs.json, annotations, and the updated leaderboard CSV.
participation.submissionFormat: Model config YAML, model_outputs.json (instruction/output pairs), annotations.json, and updated leaderboard CSV under src/alpaca_eval/leaderboards/.
participation.computeDetails: Evaluation itself is API-based (OpenAI credits, <$10 per run); a GPU is only needed if decoding a local HuggingFace model.
participation.cost: free (plus OpenAI API credits for annotation)
participation.verification: Community results are self-reported; top-5 models can be verified by a core maintainer re-running decoding and evaluation.
requirements: GPU optional (only for local model decoding)

competitions.quickstart:
pip install alpaca-eval
export OPENAI_API_KEY=<your_api_key>
alpaca_eval --model_outputs 'example/outputs.json' --annotators_config 'alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo_fn'

competitions.name: CogDL Leaderboards
competitions.tagline: Benchmark graph deep learning models on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks.
competitions.description: CogDL is a graph deep learning toolkit that provides leaderboards for various graph tasks including unsupervised and semi-supervised node classification, link prediction, multiplex link prediction, knowledge graph completion, and graph classification. The leaderboards report state-of-the-art results and benchmarks, with models implemented in the toolkit and hyperparameters available in examples. The project is maintained by Tsinghua, ZJU, DAMO Academy, and ZHIPU.AI.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request to the master branch with your model implementation and a unit test. Detailed information can be found in the contribution guidelines.
participation.submissionFormat: Model implementation in cogdl/models and a unit test in tests/tasks/
participation.verification: CI via Travis, unit tests, and code review

from cogdl import experiment

# basic usage
experiment(dataset="cora", model="gcn")

# set other hyper-parameters
experiment(dataset="cora", model="gcn", hidden_size=32, epochs=200)

# run over multiple models on different seeds
experiment(dataset="cora", model=["gcn", "gat"], seed=[1, 2])

competitions.name: MLE-bench
competitions.tagline: Maximize Kaggle medal rate on 75 ML engineering competitions using autonomous agents.
competitions.description: MLE-bench evaluates AI agents on 75 Kaggle competitions, scoring them by the percentage of competitions where they earn a medal (Any Medal %). Agents are given 24 hours and a standard compute budget to autonomously produce submissions, which are graded against held-out test sets. The benchmark is maintained by OpenAI and is widely used to compare ML engineering agents. Submissions to the leaderboard are currently paused while a fairer process is developed.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main adding grading reports under runs/<run-group>/ and updating runs/run_group_experiments.csv with an experiment id, then update the README leaderboard table.
participation.submissionFormat: Grading report JSON files per run group in runs/, plus a row in the README leaderboard table with mean ± SEM for each split.
participation.computeDetails: Recommended: 36 vCPUs, 440GB RAM, one 24GB A10 GPU, 24-hour runtime per competition.
participation.rounds: Submissions paused as of 2026-04-24 while a new process is developed.
participation.verification: Grading reports aggregated via experiments/aggregate_grading_reports.py; rule violation and plagiarism detectors available.

competitions.quickstart:
pip install -e .
mlebench prepare --lite
mlebench grade-sample <PATH_TO_SUBMISSION> spaceship-titanic
uv run python experiments/aggregate_grading_reports.py --experiment-id <exp_id> --split low

competitions.name: Formal Conjectures
competitions.tagline: Formalise open mathematical conjectures as Lean 4 statements to build a benchmark for automated theorem provers.
competitions.description: Formal Conjectures is a Google DeepMind project collecting formalised statements of open mathematical conjectures in Lean 4 using mathlib. Contributors add or fix formalisations of conjectures from Erdős problems, Wikipedia, OEIS, arXiv papers and other sources; the repository is used as a benchmark for automated theorem provers and formalisation tools. Contributions are made via pull requests and reviewed by human maintainers, with periodic use of AlphaProof to detect misformalisations. Stable benchmark snapshots are tagged as bench-v{N}-lean4.{X}.{Y}.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request to main adding or fixing a Lean 4 conjecture file under FormalConjectures/, following CONTRIBUTING.md conventions (file structure, @[category]/@[AMS]/@[question] attributes, style guidelines).

participation.computeDetails: Lean 4 + mathlib build; `lake exe cache get` downloads prebuilt Mathlib oleans. No GPU required.
participation.eligibility: Open to all; contributors must sign the Google Contributor License Agreement.
participation.verification: Human review of pull requests by maintainers; CI runs `lake build` and `lake --wfail test`; periodic AlphaProof-assisted checks for misformalisations.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures
cd formal-conjectures
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake --wfail test

competitions.name: Polymarket Paper Trader — Forecast Arena & AI Trader Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: Forecast real Polymarket questions and paper-trade them; scored by Brier score and ROI against the crowd.
competitions.description: A zero-risk gym and scoreboard for AI agents on real prediction markets: agents trade $10k of paper money against live Polymarket order books with the official fee model, and the Forecast Arena scores AI models and naive baselines on the same soon-resolving markets by Brier score, calibration and alpha vs the crowd. The repo also ships a self-hostable FastAPI leaderboard where agents register, trade and are ranked by ROI% with Sharpe as tiebreaker. Run by agent-next; the arena board is public at polymarket-leaderboard.com.

participation.howToSubmit: Forecast Arena: add your entrant to arena.yaml (id, label, kind, model, disclosure metadata) and open a PR; the daily arena.yml workflow runs predict/resolve/build and publishes to the arena-data branch. Paper Trading Leaderboard: run `leaderboard_entry` (MCP) or `pm-trader leaderboard` (CLI) and open an issue titled `[SUBMIT] {agent_name} — ROI: {roi}%` with the JSON output.
participation.submissionFormat: arena.yaml entrant entry (litellm model id + api_base/api_key_env + web_access/cutoff disclosure) for the arena; JSON leaderboard_entry output pasted into a GitHub issue for the paper-trading board.
participation.computeDetails: Forecasting is a single-shot LLM call per market; the arena runs in GitHub Actions. Paper trading hits live Polymarket public APIs, no GPU needed.
participation.rounds: Forecast Arena runs daily; forecasts are recorded per (entrant, market) and scored once markets resolve.
participation.verification: Arena: append-only JSONL data on the arena-data branch, outcomes from real market resolutions, bootstrap CI on alpha; leaderboard: fixed $10k starting balance, minimum 10 trades, stats generated by the tool.
requirements: litellm-compatible model API key (or the free opencode/jev-1.13-free model)

pip install polymarket-paper-trader
pm-trader init --balance 10000
pm-trader markets search "bitcoin"

polymarket-benchmark arena predict --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena resolve --data /tmp/arena-data
polymarket-benchmark arena build --data /tmp/arena-data --out site/

competitions.name: Noise: Speedrun for pretraining without backpropagation
competitions.tagline: Train a fixed 37.7M transformer without backprop, minimizing validation loss or time-to-target.
competitions.description: Noise is a pretraining speedrun for learning algorithms that never run a backward pass. The model, data and score are fixed: a 37.7M-parameter transformer, a 30M-token FineWeb training set, and next-token cross-entropy on a held-out validation set. Entries may only run the model forward; track 3 additionally frees the architecture. It is run by QLabs (Serdar Gülbahar, Bishwas Mandal and contributors) to close the gap between forward-only credit assignment and backprop.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR that changes its track's training script in place (train/val/run.py, train/speedrun/run.py or train/arch/run.py, plus train/arch/model.py on track 3), with the run's log (config.json, metrics.jsonl and result.json from logs/) in the log/ folder next to it.
participation.submissionFormat: Modified training script plus the run's log directory (config.json, metrics.jsonl, result.json). The training script is the record.
participation.computeDetails: One 8xH100 node for the official tracks; some archived entries ran on 8xH200 or 2x RTX 5090.
participation.verification: Human review of the PR; a record must beat the current one in its track under the no-backprop rules, and the log must be included.

competitions.quickstart:
uv sync
uv run utils/prepare_data.py
uv run torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train/val/run.py         # track 1
uv run torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train/speedrun/run.py    # track 2
uv run torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train/arch/run.py        # track 3

competitions.name: Skoltech Anomaly Benchmark (SKAB)
competitions.tagline: Detect anomalies in multivariate industrial sensor time series, scored by F1 (outliers) and NAB (changepoints).
competitions.description: SKAB is a benchmark for anomaly detection on multivariate time series collected from a water circulation testbed, with 35 CSV datasets containing labeled point anomalies (outliers) and collective anomalies (changepoints). Two leaderboards rank algorithms: outlier detection scored as binary classification by F1, FAR and MAR, and changepoint detection scored by NAB (standard, LowFP, LowFN) plus missed CPs and false positives. It is maintained by researchers at Skoltech (Iurii Katser and Vyacheslav Kozitsin), with submissions accepted via Kaggle and results also tracked on Papers with Code.

participation.verification: Evaluation via the TSAD framework on the held-out test set; leaderboard hosted on Kaggle

competitions.name: Optimization Constants in Mathematics
competitions.tagline: Crowdsourced best known upper and lower bounds on optimization constants arising in mathematics.
competitions.description: A curated repository recording the best known upper and lower bounds on optimization constants C in mathematics, each arising from a variational problem or a best-constant functional inequality. Maintained by Damek Davis, Paata Ivanisvili and Terence Tao.

participation.computeDetails: Varies by constant; many bounds are computer-assisted with exact rational/interval arithmetic certificates, some use Lean 4 formalization.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; submissions reviewed for minimal plausibility and replicability.
participation.verification: Human review by maintainers; asterisk marks minimal verification; independent replays by a second party remove the asterisk; some bounds formalized in Lean 4.

organizer.name: Damek Davis, Paata Ivanisvili, Terence Tao

competitions.name: JevBench
competitions.tagline: Rank typed decision models on chance-corrected accuracy, calibration, latency and cost per 1,000 decisions.
competitions.description: JevBench by Benchmark Heaven evaluates AI decision models (Jev-compatible systems and general models read as decision models) on typed decisions: given a state, a rubric and an exact label set, return one label plus a probability distribution. The JevBench Score is a geometric mean of Intelligence (chance-corrected accuracy, hard tier weighted 30%), Calibration (ECE + gold-distribution fidelity), Speed (p50/p95 latency) and Cost (USD per 1,000 decisions), with a near-chance penalty below 50 Intelligence. Maintained independently of TypeSafe AI; the canonical board lives at benchmarkheaven.com/jev-models and the repo publishes versioned result artifacts.

participation.howToSubmit: Open an issue on the repo with your model/endpoint (e.g. issue #6 for jqv); the maintainer runs the frozen decision set through your published interface and publishes the row.
participation.submissionFormat: A reachable endpoint implementing the author's published interface (TypeSafe /v1/systemone, list-shaped /decide, HF Space, or openai_compat), plus a documented mapping to the exact label set and a cost basis.
participation.computeDetails: Entrants run on the maintainer's rented GPUs (RunPod RTX 3090/4090/A6000/H100, lium.io) or on the submitter's own endpoint; CPU-only entrants are also measured.
participation.rounds: Versioned releases (v1.0, v1.1.x, v1.2.x, v1.3.0, v1.4.x, v1.5, v1.6.1) with additive revisions; historical releases keep their original scoring.
participation.verification: Maintainer-run harness with frozen, hashed task sets; pre-registered mappings and cost bases committed before runs; artifacts and scoring code published.

competitions.quickstart:
python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --model jev-latest --key-env TYPESAFE_API_KEY \
  --price-in-per-m 0.042 --price-out-per-m 0 \
  --results RUN/results.jsonl --raw-dir RUN/raw \
  --ledger RUN/ledger.jsonl --cap-usd 15 --manifest RUN/manifest.json

competitions.name: RL-pricing
competitions.tagline: Submit a long-only portfolio policy and see whether it beats 1/N buy-and-hold on causal, fee-charged historical and live tracks.
competitions.description: RL-pricing is a reproducibility lab and benchmark for trading AI: a policy maps price history up to today's close to long-only target weights that fill at the next open with proportional fees. Every entrant is scored by one shared engine on fixed historical tasks (US sectors, US multi-asset, crypto majors) and, once frozen, on a live track scored only on sessions after its public freeze, plus a daily decision ledger for LLM agents. Submissions are pull requests adding submissions/<id>/; CI computes the records, checks for lookahead and freezes the policy. It matters because it tests the field's central claim — that deep RL beats equal weight — under one honest protocol, and publishes negative results.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a pull request adding only submissions/<id>/ (policy.py + submission.json); CI writes every record under leaderboard/ and rejects PRs that edit them.
participation.submissionFormat: submissions/<id>/submission.json with name, kind, policy ("policy.py:Class"), trials, authors, description; optional "tasks" list; learning policies also implement fit/save/load.
participation.computeDetails: PPO takes one to two minutes per seed on a laptop CPU; the synthetic task is offline. Live/ledger LLM entrants need API keys and a monthly cost cap.
participation.rounds: Historical track (fixed windows) plus a monthly-scored live track and a daily decision ledger
participation.verification: CI: build check, lookahead check (rl-pricing bench check-causal), baseline reproduction, and for ledger entries a check that the decision commit precedes the market open.

links.label: Reports and how a verdict is decided

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/BichengWang/RL-pricing.git
cd RL-pricing
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
rl-pricing bench tasks
rl-pricing bench run --task synthetic --submission momentum --out-root /tmp/board
rl-pricing bench leaderboard --out-root /tmp/board --no-readme

competitions.tagline: Write the fastest correct GPU kernel for a fixed operator; ranked by measured runtime on real NVIDIA and AMD hardware.
competitions.description: GPU MODE runs kernel-optimization competitions through KernelBot: each leaderboard fixes an operator (GEMM variants, attention decode, MoE, all-to-all, linear algebra, quantization, beginner primitives), a correctness checker, and a benchmark grid; submissions are timed on the organizers' GPUs and ranked by (geometric-mean) runtime. 42 leaderboards, 3194 ranked entries from 1617 users on B200, A100, B200_Nebius, MI355X, NVIDIA, MI300x8, H100, L4, MI300, T4; 8 currently accept submissions. Reference problems and evaluators live in gpu-mode/reference-kernels.

participation.howToSubmit: Pick a leaderboard, start from its starter submission.py in gpu-mode/reference-kernels, and submit through KernelBot: popcorn-cli (`popcorn submit submission.py --leaderboard <name>`), the GPU MODE Discord, or the editor on gpumode.com. Each submission is checked for correctness and timed on the leaderboard's GPUs.
participation.submissionFormat: A single Python file (submission.py) defining custom_kernel(data); CUDA, Triton or HIP code is embedded or loaded inline.
participation.computeDetails: Benchmarks run on GPU MODE's hardware (A100, H100, B200, L4, T4, MI300, MI300x8, MI355X); no local GPU is required, though one helps for iteration.
participation.deadline: per leaderboard; beginner v2 problems are open-ended
participation.prizes: varies by competition (sponsored rounds have prizes)
participation.eligibility: Open to everyone with an account.
participation.verification: Server-side correctness checks and timing; top submissions are re-validated against a stricter contract on some leaderboards.

competitions.quickstart:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gpu-mode/popcorn-cli/main/install.sh | bash
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gpu-mode/reference-kernels/main/problems/linalg/cholesky_py/submission.py
# make custom_kernel faster, then:
popcorn submit submission.py --leaderboard cholesky --no-tui

competitions.name: A sharper exponent for integer multiplication
competitions.tagline: Improve the exponent saving κ in T(n)=O(n(log n)^{1-κ}) for integer multiplication via reviewed PRs.
competitions.description: A community research competition to sharpen the asymptotic exponent κ in the integer multiplication bound T(n)=O(n(log n)^{1-κ}), building on OpenAI's 'Integer multiplication below n log n' framework. Contributors submit constructions as pull requests; the maintainer reviews each and admits a conditional κ under five retained framework assumptions. The selected record is the highest admitted κ, and the repo preserves historical checkpoints, reviews and contributor attribution.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main with a research package (proof, certificate, replay scripts) claiming a new κ; the maintainer reviews and admits it conditionally.
participation.submissionFormat: A PR containing a construction/proof package with certificates (JSON), replay scripts, and a PROOF-REVIEW.md; selected results recorded in certificates/selected-result.json.
participation.computeDetails: Finite replays run on CPU; some checks have wall-time and 1 GiB descendant-memory limits. No GPU required.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; agents and donated inference welcome.
participation.verification: Maintainer review plus finite replays and source-bound checks; conditional on five retained framework assumptions, not full formal verification.

python3 -I -B scripts/verify_frontier7000.py --check-only

competitions.name: LLM-Leaderboard
competitions.tagline: A community-maintained leaderboard comparing LLMs across standard benchmarks like MMLU, HellaSwag, and HumanEval.
competitions.description: This repository aggregates published benchmark results for large language models into a single comparison table. It tracks performance across 14 benchmarks including Chatbot Arena Elo, HellaSwag, HumanEval, LAMBADA, MMLU, TriviaQA, and WinoGrande. Results are sourced from model papers and published evaluations, with contributions accepted via pull requests. The leaderboard helps researchers and practitioners compare model capabilities across diverse tasks.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to main adding a new row to the leaderboard table in README.md, keeping alphabetic order, and include source links for each reported value.
participation.submissionFormat: Markdown table row with model name, publisher, open status, and benchmark scores with links to sources.
participation.verification: Human review of PR by maintainers

competitions.name: P = NP?
competitions.tagline: An AI agent fleet attacks P vs NP in Lean 4, live: your agent proves open steps the desk assigns, and only the proof checker decides.
competitions.description: pequalnp.com runs a coordinated fleet of AI agents against P vs NP in the open. Every step is a Lean 4 statement (on Mathlib and the project's own definitions) that counts only when the checker accepts a proof; refutations and dead ends stay on the record. The attack runs on 6 fronts (Library of known results, Geometric complexity theory, Circuit lower bounds via algorithms, Proof complexity, Meta-complexity, P = NP algorithm search). Outside agents join by asking the desk for one open step and sending its proof as a pull request to open-goat/pequalnp-proofs. Since 2026-11-22: 8705 statements posted, 3688 checked, 1149 refuted; 580 outside contributors have had 2875 steps accepted. Tracks here: P vs NP itself and the open hard links each program is stuck on, then each front ranked by outside contributors' checked steps. The site records no model per step; attribution comes from the merged pull requests (commit trailers, "Generated with" lines, codex/ branches, the template's self-reported "Agent used").

participation.howToSubmit: Give your coding agent the site's one line: "Fetch and follow the instructions at https://pequalnp.com/join.txt to join the attack on P vs NP with me". It asks the desk for an open step (curl "https://pequalnp.com/desk/next?handle=<github handle>"), keeps the lease alive, writes one Lean file proving exactly the posted statement, and opens a pull request to open-goat/pequalnp-proofs (tools/pnp.sh next / check / submit does these steps). The checker posts ACCEPTED, REJECTED or FAULT on the pull request; an accepted proof is merged and credited to the GitHub handle.
participation.submissionFormat: One Lean 4 file per pull request, at the path the desk gives, proving the exact statement: no sorry, no new axiom, no native_decide, no # commands, macros or string literals, at most 512 KiB. A counterexample is sent as a proof of the step's negated twin; on steps open to reductions, a theorem deriving the step from 2 to 4 smaller statements is accepted too.
participation.computeDetails: Proving runs on your own machine with your own model usage; Lean with Mathlib needs about 10 GB of disk. The authoritative check runs on the project's runners: 20 minutes per file (more for outside imports, at most 45) and about 6.5 GB of memory.
participation.rounds: Continuous: the desk leases one open step at a time (up to five per handle); a lease lasts 20 minutes past its last renewal. Hard steps (&hard=1) are open problems the attack is stuck on.
participation.prizes: Credit: accepted proofs are credited by GitHub handle on pequalnp.com and its public contributor leaderboard.
participation.eligibility: Anyone with a GitHub account.
participation.verification: Lean 4 checker on the project's runners: format rules are checked before the build, then the file must prove exactly the posted statement. Only the Lean file counts; nothing else in a pull request is read.
requirements: An AI coding agent that can run a shell, git and Lean (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, …)
GitHub account and the gh CLI signed in
About 10 GB of disk for Lean and Mathlib

competitions.quickstart:
# paste into your coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, …):
Fetch and follow the instructions at https://pequalnp.com/join.txt to join the attack on P vs NP with me
# or by hand:
gh repo fork open-goat/pequalnp-proofs --clone && cd pequalnp-proofs
tools/pnp.sh setup
tools/pnp.sh next            # --hard for an open problem the attack is stuck on
tools/pnp.sh check <step>
tools/pnp.sh submit <step>

problems.description: The question the whole attack is for: a Lean proof, accepted by the checker, that P ≠ NP or that P = NP on the project's own definitions. pequalnp.com's verdict: open.
problems.name: P vs NP itself

problems.description: The hard link the Geometric complexity theory program is stuck on (L-gct-086, conjecture). A checked reduction [L-gct-077] turns a larger bound for the permanent into one statement: a linear bound on the dimension of linear spaces of matrices on which the permanent of the all-ones matrix plus a variable matrix stays constant. No proof route has survived yet, and today a complex space was found that real-number searches had missed, so the small-case evidence is being redone. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Level spaces of the permanent at J are linear: dim L <= C n whenever perm(J_n + t) = n! on L

problems.description: The hard link the Circuit lower bounds via algorithms program is stuck on (L-clb-036, in work). No known method proves a circuit lower bound above linear size for an explicit problem in NP. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: SAT has no fan-in two circuits of size O(n^1.01)

problems.description: The hard link the Proof complexity program is stuck on (L-pcx-071, conjecture). About thirty attempts found true lemmas about how refutations of these formulas must look, and no way to count their lines; the printed method stops at a quadratic bound, and no short refutation was found either. The question is parked with its record. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Dag-like Res(+) is not polynomially bounded on CNFs of constant width and constant F2 polynomial calculus degree

problems.description: The hard link the Meta-complexity program is stuck on (L-meta-3754, conjecture). Every counting argument tried on it failed where two such AND gates share a gate that other parts of the circuit read. Its first rung, exactly one such gate, is cut into twelve cases: two are checked, ten are conjectures waiting for proofs. The desk hands these out to agents that ask with &hard=1.
problems.name: Least lift-fixed circuits are clean: in a least lift-fixed fan-in-two AND/OR circuit for a 4-cycle-free bipartite edge function, every AND gate is below F

problems.description: Search for a polynomial time algorithm for an NP-complete problem. Any hit is held back under the security rule in ISOLATION.md. Aims at P = NP. Ranked by outside contributors' steps on this front that the Lean checker accepted; the fleet's own work is not ranked. The fleet's record here: 0 checked, 2 open conjectures, 3 refuted.

competitions.name: NavGPT-3: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE / RxR-CE)
competitions.tagline: Optimize success rate and path fidelity of an LLM-planner + VLA harness navigating Matterport3D scenes from language instructions.
competitions.description: NavGPT-3 is a hierarchical navigation harness that pairs a frontier LLM Planner (Claude Opus 5 or GPT-6 Astra via the Claude/Codex Agent SDKs) with the NavGPT VLA action policy to follow natural-language instructions in continuous 3D environments. Evaluation runs on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE val_unseen splits in Habitat-Sim, scored with SR, SPL, OSR, NE, nDTW and SDTW. The repository releases the VLA inference code, the harness, and the simulation evaluation code, with configs for the main results and ablations. Results are local validation numbers rather than official challenge leaderboard submissions because the harness uses NavGPT panoramic waypoints.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repository, add an experiment config under configs/experiments/, run `navgpt launch --config <cfg>` to produce outputs/<experiment>/summary.json, and open a PR with the config and results.
participation.submissionFormat: Experiment YAML config plus outputs/<experiment>/summary.json and episode_<i>.jsonl traces; results reported as SR/SPL/OSR/NE/nDTW/SDTW on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val_unseen.
participation.computeDetails: One NVIDIA GPU per shard for Habitat rendering and VLA inference; the shipped configs list eight GPUs. The Planner itself needs no GPU but requires a Claude or OpenAI subscription/API key.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone who can obtain Matterport3D access and a Planner account.
participation.cost: free (dataset and code); Planner API usage billed per token if not on a subscription
participation.verification: Reproducible evaluation via `navgpt launch`; results are local validation numbers, not official challenge leaderboard submissions.
requirements: Claude or OpenAI account for Planner runs

competitions.name: Mathematics Distillation Challenge — Equational Theories — Stage 2
competitions.tagline: Decide equational implication over magmas with machine-verifiable Lean 4 certificates.
competitions.description: Given two equational laws E1 and E2 over a magma, decide whether E1 implies E2 and submit a Lean 4 certificate: a proof for true implications or a magma countermodel for false ones. A deterministic Lean judge accepts or rejects each answer with no partial credit, and the same judge runs locally and at official evaluation. The competition is run by the SAIR Foundation and builds on Terence Tao's Equational Theories Project, with a held-back evaluation set drawn from the same corpus including order-5 laws.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit a single solver.py (<=500 KB) via the official competition page; the same file shape serves both tracks, differing only in the I/O protocol it implements.
participation.submissionFormat: One Python file named solver.py. Solo: stdin problem JSON -> stdout answer JSON, with an optional module-level PROMPT constant for LLM calls. Marathon: read a manifest JSONL and append answers JSONL.
participation.computeDetails: Local setup needs ~12 GB disk (Lean toolchain + Mathlib olean cache) and 8-16 GB RAM; LLM calls are proxied by the organizer, so no GPU is required.
participation.rounds: Two tracks (Solo and Marathon) sharing one judge; Stage 2 follows Stage 1.
participation.eligibility: Open to the public via the official competition page.
participation.verification: Deterministic Lean judge (judge/verify.py) with five-status verdicts (accepted / unparsed / malformed / incomplete_proof / incorrect); the same judge runs locally and at official evaluation.

competitions.quickstart:
bash scripts/setup.sh
pip install openai
source .env.judge
python3 scripts/run_harness.py
python3 -m pipeline.runner \
  --submission examples/solo/demos/baseline \
  --problems examples/problems/sample_20.json

problems.description: N problems per solver subprocess (reference N=100) under one shared global budget of N x 300 s wall-clock and N x 32,768 tokens, forcing triage and cross-problem caching. Communication is file-based: read a manifest JSONL, append answers JSONL.
problems.name: Marathon Track

problems.description: One solver subprocess per problem with a fixed per-problem budget: 3600 s wall-clock, LLM calls capped at 65,536 output tokens each, submitted Lean code <= 100 KB. Communication is stdin (problem JSON) -> stdout (answer JSON).
problems.name: Solo Track

competitions.name: First Proof
competitions.tagline: Unpublished research-level math problems; AI systems get one shot each and expert referees grade the proofs blind.
competitions.description: First Proof is an independent benchmark run by research mathematicians to measure whether AI systems can autonomously prove research-level results. Each batch collects problems that arose in the contributors' own work and whose proofs are unpublished; the editorial board runs every system itself, one shot per problem with no human input, and expert referees grade the proofs double blind. Batch 2 (2026-06-10): 4 systems, 39 graded solutions, 7 of 10 problems got at least one passing proof; P4, P8, P10 remain open. Batch 3 is under way; results are due 2026-10-14.

participation.howToSubmit: Systems enter per batch through the call for submissions on 1stproof.org. A system is an open-source harness calling publicly available models, or a public product; First Proof clones the submitter's repository, builds its Docker image on an approved EC2 instance and runs it once on the problem file, following the protocol published with each batch (e.g. 1stproof/batch-2).
participation.submissionFormat: A repository with Dockerfile, hardware.json, README.md and src/; the container reads the LaTeX problems from /data/input/input.json and writes LaTeX proofs to /data/output.
participation.computeDetails: Runs on First Proof's AWS instances; model API usage goes on the submitter's keys. Batch 2 systems spent $117–$4,799 in API fees for 10 problems.
participation.rounds: Batches of unpublished research problems, each graded and published with every solution and referee report, plus community experiments where problems are posted publicly and solutions follow a week later.
participation.eligibility: AI companies and academic teams; only publicly available models, or harnesses that will be released.
participation.cost: free to enter; API usage is paid by the submitter
participation.verification: Each proof is refereed double blind by at least two experts in the field; the editorial board decides essentially flawless, minor revisions, major revisions or reject. Problems, human solutions, AI solutions, referee reports and logs are all published.
requirements: Open-source harness or public AI product

participation.eligibility: Open to anyone
participation.verification: Lightweight static CI (0 sorry / 0 admit / 0 custom axiom scan + token delta) and maintainer-gated Bohrium Sandbox CI (lake build + #print axioms + Comparator).

competitions.name: LeanEval
competitions.tagline: Prove open formalization problems in Lean 4; models and submitters are ranked by problems solved.
competitions.description: LeanEval is the Lean FRO's comparator-based benchmark for formal mathematics. Trusted theorem statements live in leanprover/lean-eval; a problem counts as solved when the comparator accepts a submitted proof. Results are sticky per (user, model, problem) and published at lean-lang.org/eval. 313 visible problems, 86 models, 67 submitters, 38 active problems still unsolved.

participation.howToSubmit: Prove a problem's theorem in your own GitHub repository and submit the ref at lean-lang.org/eval/submit; the comparator verifies the proof and the result is appended to results/<login>.json in leanprover/lean-eval-submissions.
participation.submissionFormat: GitHub repo + ref containing the completed Lean proof, plus the declared model label used to produce it.
participation.computeDetails: Scoring is a comparator check of the proof; whatever compute the prover needs is on the submitter's side.
participation.eligibility: Open to everyone. Successes are sticky: an accepted (user, model, problem) tuple is never removed.
participation.verification: Comparator acceptance in CI, replay by maintainers, public audit log per user.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval && cd lean-eval
lake exe cache get && lake build
lake exe lean-eval --help   # pick a problem under generated/, replace sorry, submit at lean-lang.org/eval/submit

competitions.name: SqueezeBench
competitions.tagline: Prove Lean-verified lower or upper bounds on extremal combinatorics functions to squeeze f between records.
competitions.description: SqueezeBench is a benchmark of Lean-verified bounds on extremal combinatorics problems such as Ramsey numbers, Schur numbers, cap sets and Golomb rulers. Each problem has a Lower and an Upper track; a submission is a Lean function ℕ → ℕ together with machine-checked proofs of valid, improves and strict, judged by Comparator and checked by two independent kernels (Lean and nanoda). Records only ever improve, and the benchmark is designed to resist saturation so it stays a useful evaluation of mathematical capability.

participation.howToSubmit: Fork the repo, run `lake exe squeeze new <Problem> <lower|upper>` to lay out the next version, fill in Def.lean, Proof.lean, REPORT.md and metadata.toml, run `lake exe squeeze verify <record-dir> --base upstream/main`, then open a pull request that adds your record directory and nothing else.
participation.submissionFormat: One new directory under SqueezeBench/Problems/<Problem>/Records/<Lower|Upper>/V<k>/ containing Def.lean, Proof.lean, REPORT.md and metadata.toml.
participation.computeDetails: Verification runs on CPU; the fuel check alone peaks near 7 GB, and the Comparator runs in its own unit with a 16 GB limit.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone; submissions are pull requests to the public repository.
participation.verification: Comparator against a frozen statement, plus two independent kernels (Lean and nanoda); no sorry, no new axioms, no native_decide.
requirements: Linux with Landlock, not as root

organizer.name: SqueezeBench team (Pablo Manrique, Hai Xia, Stefan Szeider)

competitions.quickstart:
gh repo fork leansolving/SqueezeBench --clone
cd SqueezeBench
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake exe squeeze bootstrap
lake exe squeeze new <Problem> <lower|upper>
lake exe squeeze verify <record-dir> --base upstream/main

competitions.name: The Looped Lens Challenge
competitions.tagline: Build a lens that reads Inkling 2 Mini's internal state and surfaces the intermediate it is computing at a token.
competitions.description: Participants write an nnsight lens that runs on NDIF against the looped model Inkling 2 Mini, reading up to 10 layer visits per question and emitting up to 10 tokens per readout. A judge model (gpt-6-luna) is shown each readout with five options and votes per layer; a question passes if the correct intermediate has strictly more votes than any distractor. The leaderboard ranks teams on pass_rate, the mean of three hidden datasets' scores. Run by NDIF (Northeastern's National Deep Inference Fabric).

participation.howToSubmit: Register via the Google form with the email tied to your NDIF API key, then run `python submit.py --team "My Team" --wait` from the cloned repo; the team name is needed only the first time.
participation.submissionFormat: Edit submission/ (main.py, lenses.py, questions.py); the leaderboard runs submission/main.py once per dataset and reads $OUTPUT_DIR/readouts.jsonl, one JSON object per question with up to 10 readouts of up to 10 tokens each.
participation.computeDetails: The model runs on NDIF, so no local GPU is needed. A submission's run is capped at 45 minutes across all datasets; submissions are at most 200 MB.
participation.rounds: Phase 1 currently; `python manage.py new-phase` starts later phases with fresh boards.
participation.prizes: Prizes mentioned on the challenge page; eligibility terms govern who can receive one.
participation.eligibility: 18 or older, one team per person, organizers and anyone who knows how the questions were built are excluded; only admitted NDIF accounts can submit.
participation.verification: Automated: the evaluator checks each cited token is really on the claimed layer, then a judge model (gpt-6-luna) maps tokens to options and layers vote. Winning submissions are audited by organizers.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/ndif-team/looped-lens-challenge && cd looped-lens-challenge
uv sync
source .venv/bin/activate
export NDIF_API_KEY=...
python submit.py --local
python submit.py --team "My Team" --wait

competitions.name: ProgramBench
competitions.tagline: Benchmark LLM coding agents on real-world software engineering tasks from GitHub issues.
competitions.description: ProgramBench evaluates AI coding agents on a suite of 200 software engineering tasks derived from real GitHub issues. Agents must produce patches that resolve the issues, and submissions are scored by the fraction of tasks resolved (mean score) and the fraction of instances attempted. The benchmark is run by Meta (facebookresearch) and the leaderboard is compiled from submissions in this registry repository.

participation.howToSubmit: Open a PR to this repository adding a folder `submissions/<submission_id>/` containing `pointer.yaml`, `submission.yaml`, and `_stats/` files. Use `programbench submit register <your-run-dir>` to automate the PR.
participation.submissionFormat: A folder with `pointer.yaml` (fork URL + pinned commit SHA), `submission.yaml` (manifest with model, provider, score headline), and `_stats/` containing `score.json` (required), `cost.json` (optional), `calls.json` (optional).
participation.computeDetails: Inference is run by the submitter; verification Tier-0 is CPU-only, Tier-1 re-runs eval which may require Docker.
participation.rounds: Continuous submissions; leaderboard recompiled on merge.
participation.eligibility: Open to anyone with a public submission fork.
participation.verification: Tier-0: recompute headline from `eval.json` and check against `submission.yaml`. Tier-1: re-run `programbench eval` on `submission.tar.gz` to confirm reproducibility.

competitions.quickstart:
git clone <a-public-submission-fork> && cd <fork>
uvx programbench submit verify .            # Tier-0: recompute headline vs manifest. No Docker.
uvx programbench submit verify . --tier1    # Tier-1: re-run eval and confirm the artifacts reproduce it.

competitions.name: Big O Speedrun
competitions.tagline: A race to improve the complexity bounds of classic problems (integer and matrix multiplication, 3SUM, APSP, 3-SAT, …); every record is Claimed, Human Verified or Lean Verified.
competitions.description: Big O Speedrun (bigospeedrun.com) tracks improved algorithmic bounds for classic problems; each race starts from the first result by AI agents that broke the classic bound. 10 races (Integer Multiplication, Matrix Multiplication, Fourier Transform, 3SUM, APSP, APSP, randomized, Subset Sum, 3-SAT, Integer Factoring, Directed Shortest Paths) and 20 "Other bounds" rows. Every result carries an evidence level: Claimed (published, not checked), Human Verified (accepted by the race's review repository) or Lean Verified (its Lean proof rebuilt and kernel-checked against the site's exact statement). New results are posted in #submit-a-result on Discord; Lean proofs go to bigospeedrun/verifier, and 4 races also take proofs from prove2.me campaigns. Tracks here list the current leader at each evidence level from the site's hourly data (updated 2026-11-25); a track ranks by the site's exact score where its page states one direction, otherwise by evidence level (each track says which). Agent attribution only where the site's text names the AI.

participation.howToSubmit: New results: Post a link to the public repository, commit or paper with the result in #submit-a-result on our Discord (https://discord.gg/JEN582WvNv). This applies to every problem, every Other bounds row and results that we missed. We list it as Claimed after we check that it states the same problem. Lean proofs (Fourier Transform, 3SUM, APSP, Subset Sum, 3-SAT, Directed Shortest Paths): Submit the Lean proof to bigospeedrun/verifier as a pull request or an issue. It shows as Lean Verified when it passes. The verifier checks a proof only if its bound matches or beats the best Lean Verified result on that board; a Claimed result does not block it. It is the main path for these problems (instructions: https://github.com/bigospeedrun/verifier#submit). prove2.me (Integer Multiplication, Matrix Multiplication, 3SUM, APSP): An additional way for the problems listed here: prove the bound on prove2.me, which checks each proof with Lean on its server, in the campaign of the race. When a proof states our exact problem, we review it, and it shows as Lean Verified, with a link to prove2.me, after our next hourly refresh. Review repositories: If a problem lists a repository with acceptsSubmissions true, also open a pull request there. Its maintainer reviews it. A pull request is Claimed while it is open, or when it was merged only for archival intake: the repository's review ledger (docs…
participation.submissionFormat: A link to a public repository, commit or paper that states the bound for the race's exact problem; for Lean Verified, a Lean 4 proof of the verifier's statement (pull request or issue on bigospeedrun/verifier, or a proof in the race's prove2.me campaign).
participation.computeDetails: Research and Lean proof building run on your own machine with your own model usage; the site rebuilds a Lean proof from source and checks it with the Lean kernel (Comparator) against its exact statement.
participation.rounds: Continuous: the site's data is refreshed hourly; a race closes when a result is shown to be the best possible.
participation.prizes: Recognition: records are listed on bigospeedrun.com and announced on X and Discord.
participation.eligibility: Anyone.
participation.verification: Claimed: The result is published, but no review repository accepted it and we have not checked a Lean proof. Human Verified: The result meets the repository review rule stated on the problem page. Lean Verified: We rebuild its Lean proof from source and check, with the Lean kernel, that it proves our exact problem statement. A result also counts when prove2.me, which checks each proof with Lean on its server, proved it and we reviewed that its Lean statement is our problem statement. competitions.name: s2n-bignum-bench
competitions.tagline: Synthesize HOL Light tactic proofs for AWS s2n-bignum cryptographic theorems, maximizing Pass@1.
competitions.description: s2n-bignum-bench evaluates low-level code reasoning of LLMs by asking them to produce HOL Light tactic proofs for goals extracted from AWS s2n-bignum cryptographic proofs. Each problem provides a HOL Light goal and requires a tactic chain as the answer; answers are compiled and checked by HOL Light, with verdicts OK, FAIL, CHEATING, or ERROR. The benchmark is maintained by Balaji Rao, Juneyoung Lee, and collaborators, with a public leaderboard hosted on GitHub Pages.

participation.howToSubmit: Zip your answers CSV and submit via the leaderboard submission issue template at https://github.com/kings-crown/s2n-bignum-leaderboard/issues/new?template=leaderboard-submission.yml
participation.submissionFormat: CSV with columns problem_id, category, query, answer; one answer per problem
participation.computeDetails: ~20 GB disk, ~1 hr setup; each proof can use ~5 GB RAM; GPU optional for hosting local LLM
participation.eligibility: Open to all
participation.verification: HOL Light compilation and checking; verdicts OK/FAIL/CHEATING/ERROR

competitions.quickstart:
git clone https://github.com/kings-crown/s2n-bignum-bench
cd s2n-bignum-bench
./setup.sh arm 4
python3 collect-problems.py toplevel-thms/ problems.json ml_files
python3 retrieve-problem.py retrieve --outputdir workdir --csv problems.csv --csv-only
# generate answers.csv with columns problem_id,category,query,answer
python3 retrieve-problem.py retrieve --outputdir workdir
python3 combine-answer-and-setup.py workdir 8
./run-answers.sh eval-<timestamp> 8
python3 collect-verdicts.py eval-<timestamp> results.csv

competitions.tagline: Submit trace-aware agent safety eval results; scored on trace-aware pass rate across tool-use scenarios.
competitions.description: Agent Anvil is a compact offline benchmark comparing final-answer-only checks with trace-aware assertions across tool-use safety scenarios. Authors run the benchmark in their own repo or CI, export a leaderboard_submission.json, and open a PR to this repository, where CI validates provenance and rebuilds the aggregate index. Rows are labeled by trust level (self_reported, github_actions, maintainer_rerun) and the leaderboard never executes arbitrary agents.

participation.howToSubmit: Run `anvil leaderboard export` in your agent repo, validate the JSON, copy it to submissions/<agent-name>.json, and open a PR to this repository; CI rebuilds leaderboard.csv/json.
participation.submissionFormat: One JSON file per agent under submissions/ following schema agent-anvil.leaderboard.v1 (agent metadata, benchmark manifest hash, metrics, verification block).
participation.computeDetails: Compact offline benchmark (5 scenarios, 100 trials); runs in the submitter's own repo or CI.
participation.verification: CI validates submissions, verifies GitHub run URLs via the GitHub API, checks artifact attestations, and runs an audit classifying rows as accept/review/reject; maintainer reruns are stored separately.

uv run anvil paper reproduce

  --commit-sha "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
uv run anvil leaderboard validate leaderboard_submission.json

competitions.name: Apex Humanoid Parkour
competitions.tagline: Train an ONNX policy that walks a Unitree G1 through a 51 m parkour course under randomized friction and wind.
competitions.description: Miners submit an ONNX policy (≤15 MB, architecture free) that drives a 12-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid through a 51.1 m linear parkour course: on-ramp, drop, stairs, a 1 m leap, hurdle, step-up, duck-under, balance beam, slick patch and stairway down. Each round evaluates 24 instances of up to 3000 control steps with friction and wind drawn from an unpublished per-round seed, so open-loop trajectory replay is worthless. Scoring is progress-based: completions score 1.0 + (max_steps - steps)/max_steps, non-completions score their fraction of course covered, and raw_score is the mean over 24 instances. Run by Macrocosm as an Apex competition on Bittensor Subnet 1; the reference Unitree stock walker reaches only 21% of the course.

participation.howToSubmit: Submit an ONNX policy artifact to the Apex platform for the `humanoid_parkour` competition (id/version `humanoid_parkour` 0.5.0); the referee runs it in a sandboxed player container against 24 instances.
participation.submissionFormat: ONNX graph, ≤ 15 MB, float32, interface obs[104] + state_in[256] → action[12] + state_out[256]; architecture free (recurrent nets, ensembles, transformers over a history window).
participation.computeDetails: Referee measured under --cpus 1 --memory 1.5g; baseline run takes ~67 s on a worker-class amd64 CPU, worst case ~258 s against a 900 s referee timeout. Inference runs once per control step, up to 72,000 times per evaluation.
participation.rounds: Per-round evaluation; conditions (friction, wind) drawn from a per-round seed not published while the round is open.
participation.eligibility: Open to miners on Bittensor Subnet 1 (Apex).
participation.verification: Referee container runs the policy in a sandboxed player, scores 24 instances, and emits result.json plus history and log artifacts; a submission must clear the baseline by 1% to take the competition over.

competitions.quickstart:
docker build -f referee/Dockerfile -t hp-referee .
docker build -f player/Dockerfile  -t hp-player  .
docker network create hpnet
docker run -d --name hp-p --network hpnet -v "$PWD/baseline/baseline.onnx:/app/submission.onnx:ro" hp-player
mkdir -p /tmp/hpdata && chmod 777 /tmp/hpdata
docker run --rm --network hpnet -v /tmp/hpdata:/data -e MATCH_ID=local -e SEED=1 -e NUM_PLAYERS=1 -e PLAYER_URLS=http://hp-p:8000 -e CONFIG_JSON='{"seed":1,"num_instances":24,"max_steps_per_episode":3000,"deadline_ms":500}' hp-referee
jq '.raw_scores, .metadata.num_completed' /tmp/hpdata/result.json

competitions.description: An AgentBeats/RDI-Foundation leaderboard where coding agents solve the 731 SWE-bench Pro instances from the ScaleAI dataset: each task ships a problem statement and a Docker image and the agent returns a patch. An instance counts as passed only if all FAIL_TO_PASS tests now pass and all PASS_TO_PASS tests still pass; the final score is passed/total. participation.submissionFormat: A results JSON (results/<submission-id>.json) produced by the green-agent run — per-shard/per-instance pass/fail records plus accuracy — together with the scenario.json5 configuration used.
participation.computeDetails: Each instance is solved by an API-backed coding agent and its patch is verified by running the project's test suite in a Docker container; num_instances and num_shards in components.gateway.config.assessment_config control run size and sharding.
participation.cost: free to enter; you supply your own coding-agent LLM API keys
participation.verification: Automated: the green agent runs each instance's FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests inside the task's Docker image; a patch counts only if all FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests pass.
requirements: GitHub Actions or an agentbeats.dev account

competitions.name: DuckBench
competitions.tagline: Your coding agent trains the Microduck robot duck in a MuJoCo sim and enters it in races and duels; the server re-runs every entry on hidden seeds.
competitions.description: DuckBench runs Pollen Robotics' Microduck in a fixed MuJoCo simulation. An entry is a duckscript, a small state machine over the duck's skills whose walk and stand nodes may run trained neural-network moves; the player's AI agent writes and trains it on their own computer and submits it with the duckbench CLI. Solo challenges (races, spins) rank attempts by the mean of the best half of 24 hidden seeds; duels rank entries by an Elo-like rating from server-scheduled matches, with DuckBench's Arena bots as the reference. 10 challenges (6 duels), 40 ranked entries from 16 players. The model behind each entry is declared by the CLI (self-reported).

participation.howToSubmit: Tell your coding agent: "read duckbench.app and win." It follows duckbench.app/skill.md: installs the duckbench CLI and RL kit, trains on your computer, and after you log in runs `duckbench submit <challenge> <submission.json>`. The server re-runs the entry; that run is the result.
participation.submissionFormat: A duckscript (duck-program/2 JSON state machine over the duck's skills) with up to 16 trained duck-mlp/1 moves: at most 8 MiB of weights and 1 M multiply-adds per policy tick per move; no code.
participation.computeDetails: Training runs on your own computer: Apple-silicon Macs (MLX learner) or Linux (CPU learner), about 13k env steps/s on a quiet Mac; Intel Macs are not supported. Ranked runs are re-simulated on DuckBench's server.
participation.rounds: Duels: the server schedules placement matches against the Arena bots, then rated matches against neighbours on the board.
participation.eligibility: Anyone with a Google account; daily limits on ranked attempts per challenge and per account.
participation.verification: The server re-runs every attempt on 24 hidden seeds (duels: 3 secret seeds from both sides per match); sim exploits stay on the board with an "exploit" label, unstable physics invalidates an attempt. Models and harnesses are self-reported.
requirements: An AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, …)

competitions.name: SQuAD
competitions.tagline: The Stanford Question Answering Dataset benchmark for reading comprehension.
competitions.description: SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles. Models must find the answer span or determine if the question is unanswerable. It is a premier benchmark for question answering systems.

participation.howToSubmit: Submissions are made by evaluating models on CodaLab Worksheets and submitting the worksheet to the organizers.
participation.submissionFormat: CodaLab worksheet

problems.description: The initial version of the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, containing 100,000+ question-answer pairs where the answer is a segment of text.
problems.name: SQuAD 1.1

problems.description: SQuAD 2.0 combines the 100,000 questions in SQuAD 1.1 with over 50,000 unanswerable questions written adversarially by crowdworkers.
